To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a significant number of women receiving treatment for recurrent major depression report an insecure attachment profile, which is associated with interpersonal difficulties that remain salient during both acute depressive episodes and following recovery.

a high proportion of women with recurrent major depressive disorder have Fearful Avoidant adult attachment patterns, and that these women have more interpersonal difficulties than women with other attachment styles.

a high level of Fearful Avoidant adult attachment is associated with greater interpersonal difficulties and lower levels of self esteem, and is predictive of a longer time to remission in women with recurrent depression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how adult attachment profiles may affect the course and outcome of interpersonal psychotherapy for major depression.
the clinical utility of adult attachment theory in the assessment and treatment of depression.
the role of attachment in the development and course of depression, and the implications of attachment for treatment response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attachment insecurity, particularly Fearful Avoidant patterns, is not a barrier to successful treatment with interpersonal psychotherapy for major depressive disorder.

the Fearful Avoidant group of attachment styles are associated with more negative attitudes toward themselves, others, and interpersonal difficulties, which remain salient both during the acute depressive episode and after the acute depressive episode remitted.

the results of this study indicate that attachment insecurity is associated with interpersonal difficulties and poorer response to interpersonal psychotherapeutic treatment in women with recurrent depression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
women with Fearful Avoidant adult attachment patterns are likely to experience heightened interpersonal difficulties, even when not actively depressed.
attachment insecurity may be a marker for interpersonal difficulties and a risk factor for poor treatment response.
women who report high levels of Fearful Avoidant interpersonal difficulties during a major depression may be at risk for a more protracted course of illness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women with recurrent major depressive disorder who are characterized by high Fearful Avoidance may be more likely to experience difficulties with interpersonal relationships.
a significant proportion of women with recurrent major depressive disorder present with a ‘Fearful avoidant’ attachment style.
a Fearful Avoidant interpersonal profile is associated with greater interpersonal difficulties and a more protracted time to stabilization among IPT remitting women.
